{{Short description|Interpretation rule in formal semantics}}
In [[formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics]], a '''type shifter''' is an [[compositionality|interpretation]] rule that changes an expression's [[type theory|semantic type]]. For instance, the [[English language|English]] expression "John" might ordinarily [[denotation|denote]] John himself, but a type shifting rule called {{Smallcaps|Lift}} can raise its denotation to a [[function (mathematics)|function]] which takes a property and returns "true" if John himself has that property. Lift can be seen as mapping an individual onto the [[principal ultrafilter]] that it generates.<ref name= "pr83">{{cite encyclopedia |last1=Partee |first1=Barbara |author-link1=Barbara Partee | last2=Rooth |first2=Mats |author-link2=Mats Rooth |editor-last1=Portner |editor-first1=Paul | editor-last2=Partee |editor-first2=Barbara |encyclopedia= Formal semantics: The essential readings |title= Generalized conjunction and type ambiguity |url=https://semanticsarchive.net/Archive/ThiYWY5Y/BHP_Rooth83Generalized%20Conjunction.pdf |year=1983 |publisher=Wiley|doi=10.1002/9780470758335.ch14 |pages= 334–356 |isbn=9780470758335 }}</ref><ref name = "p83">{{cite encyclopedia |last1=Partee |first1=Barbara |author-link1=Barbara Partee|editor-last1=Portner |editor-first1=Paul | editor-last2=Partee |editor-first2=Barbara |encyclopedia= Formal semantics: The essential readings |title= Noun phrase interpretation and type shifting principles |url=http://eecoppock.info/CompositionalSemantics/Partee-Type-Shifting.pdf |year=1983 |publisher=Wiley|doi=10.1002/9780470758335.ch15 |pages= 357–381 |isbn=9780470758335 }}</ref><ref name = "hk4">{{cite book |last1=Heim |first1=Irene | last2=Kratzer | first2=Angelika |author-link1=Irene Heim |author-link2=Angelika Kratzer |date=1998 |title=Semantics in Generative Grammar |publisher=Wiley Blackwell | location = Oxford|at=Chapter 4}}</ref>

# Without type shifting: <math> \, \, [\![John]\!] = j </math>
# Type shifting with {{Smallcaps|Lift}}: <math>[\![John]\!] = \lambda P_{\langle e,t \rangle} . P(j) </math>

Type shifters were proposed by [[Barbara Partee]] and [[Mats Rooth]] in 1983 to allow for systematic type [[ambiguity]]. Work of the period assumed that [[syntactic category|syntactic categories]] corresponded directly with semantic types, and researchers thus had to "generalize to the worst case" when particular uses of particular expressions from a given category required an especially high type. Moreover, Partee argued that evidence, in fact, supported expressions having different types in different contexts. Thus, she and Rooth proposed type shifting as a principled mechanism for generating the ambiguity.<ref name = "pr83"/><ref name = "p83" /><ref name = hk4 />

Type shifters remain a standard tool in formal semantic work, particularly in [[categorial grammar]] and related frameworks. Type shifters have also been used to interpret quantifiers in object position and to capture [[scope (formal semantics)|scope ambiguities]]. In that regard, they serve as an alternative to syntactic operations such as [[quantifier raising]] used in mainstream [[generative grammar|generative]] approaches to semantics. <ref>{{cite book |last1=Heim |first1=Irene | last2=Kratzer | first2=Angelika |author-link1=Irene Heim |author-link2=Angelika Kratzer |date=1998 |title=Semantics in Generative Grammar |publisher=Wiley Blackwell | location = Oxford |pages= 184–188}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Jacobson |first=Pauline |author-link= |year=2014 |title= Compositional semantics: An introduction to the syntax/semantics interface |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780199677153}}</ref> Type shifters have also been used to generate and [[compositionality|compose]] alternative sets without the need to fully adopt an [[alternative semantics|alternative-based semantics]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Charlow |first1=Simon |title=Alternatives via scope |journal=Unpublished Course Notes |year=2015|url=https://simoncharlow.com/courses/alts/handouts/week10.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Charlow |first1=Simon|year=2020 |title= The scope of alternatives: Indefiniteness and islands |url=https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/003302 |journal= Linguistics and Philosophy |volume=43 |issue=4|pages=427–472 |doi=10.1007/s10988-019-09278-3|s2cid=254749307|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
